- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message ending with:
   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.

   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Vedaksha: Vedic Astrology & Ephemeris Engine

## Purpose
Vedaksha is a specialized computational system for generating astrological charts and astronomical calculations grounded in Vedic traditions. It targets both human users seeking natal chart analysis and AI agents requiring precise celestial data.

## Tech Stack
- **Primary Language:** Rust (with sub-arcsecond precision algorithms)
- **Data Sources:** JPL DE440s/DE441 kernels, VSOP87A analytical series, ELP/MPP02 lunar theory
- **Distribution:** Python bindings, WebAssembly for browsers, native Rust libraries
- **Integration:** Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI agent connectivity

## Main Features

**Astronomical Capabilities:**
- Sub-arcsecond planetary position accuracy (mean 0.103″ vs JPL Horizons, 1900–2025)
- Dual ephemeris paths: kernel-based (SpkReader) and analytical (AnalyticalProvider for edge/WASM)
- Precession, nutation, light-time, and ΔT corrections

**Vedic Astrology:**
The system computes "kundali (natal charts), panchanga, dashas, nakshatras, vargas" with 27 nakshatras, 5 dasha systems, 16 varga divisional charts, six-component shadbala calculations, and 11 ayanamsha options—each derived from documented primary sources.

**Western Astrology:**
House systems, aspects with applying/separating motion, essential dignities, synastry, and composite charts.

**Integration Layer:**
Converts charts into property graphs queryable via Cypher/SurrealQL, enabling semantic agent reasoning about planetary relationships.

## Architecture

The engine organizes into published Rust crates: `vedaksha` (umbrella), `-math`, `-ephem-core`, `-astro`, `-vedic`, `-graph`, and `-mcp`. Each chart computation returns typed structs; graph emission is a separate, queryable projection. The MCP server exposes 17 tools—from `compute_natal_chart` to `emit_graph`—discoverable and version-locked via snapshot tests.

## Licensing & Status
Currently under Business Source License 1.1 (BUSL-1.1), converting to Apache 2.0 four years post-release. Non-commercial use is free; commercial licensing costs $500 per organization. The project includes 24,350 validated test oracle rows and extensive clean-room audit documentation.

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using Glob, Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.

## The big picture

You give the program: **date of birth, time of birth, place of birth**. It calculates where all the planets actually were in the sky at that moment, converts that into a **Vedic birth chart (kundali)** drawn in **South Indian square style**, plus supporting info (nakshatra, dasha periods, panchanga). Everything runs **on your machine, no internet required** — the astronomical data lives in files on your disk, not on a server.

## The 4 building blocks (layers)

Think of it like a pipeline, each stage doing one job and handing off to the next:

**1. Ephemeris layer — "where are the planets?"**
This is pure astronomy, no astrology yet. Given a date/time/location, it answers "the Sun is at 15.3° Sagittarius, Mars is at 2.1° Leo," etc.
- **Library: `pyswisseph`** (Swiss Ephemeris) — this is the same engine virtually all professional Vedic astrology software uses. It works fully offline.

**2. Astrology logic layer — "what does that mean in Vedic terms?"**
Takes the raw planet positions and turns them into:
- Rashi (which of the 12 zodiac signs each planet is in)
- Bhava (which of the 12 houses, based on your ascendant/lagna)
- Nakshatra + pada (27 lunar mansions, used heavily in Vedic astrology)
- Navamsa (D9) chart — a commonly-used secondary chart
- Panchanga (tithi, vara, yoga, karana — the 5 daily almanac elements)
- Vimshottari Dasha — the planetary period timeline used for predictions
This is the part I write myself — it's rules/formulas applied to the data from layer 1, no external library does this specifically for Vedic astrology.

**3. Chart rendering layer — "draw it"**
Takes the house/planet data and draws it as a **South Indian style chart**: a fixed 4×4 grid (minus the center 2×2) where each square is always the same zodiac sign, and your ascendant sign gets marked.

**4. Interface layer — "how you interact with it"**
- **CLI** (command line tool) — you type in birth details, get a chart printed/saved.
- **MCP server** — lets Claude (or another AI agent) call your chart engine directly as a tool, so you could ask an agent "generate my chart" instead of running the CLI yourself. Still 100% local — MCP just means "a program can call this tool," not "this talks to the internet."

| Tool | Job |
|---|---|
| `pydantic` | Defines the shape of data (e.g. "a Planet has a name, a sign, a degree") and catches mistakes early |
| `pytest` | Automated tests — checks our calculations against known-correct chart examples so we catch bugs |
| `typer` | Builds the CLI (the `python -m vedaksha_clone --dob ... --tob ... --place ...` command) |
| `pyproject.toml` | Standard Python packaging so the project installs cleanly |

2. **Rashi + Bhava + Ascendant** — turn positions into signs/houses. Test against a known chart again.

# Local Vedic Astrology Chart Engine (Phase 1)

## Context

The user wants to build a project inspired by [arthiqlabs/vedaksha](https://github.com/arthiqlabs/vedaksha) (a Rust-based Vedic astrology + ephemeris engine with an MCP server for AI agents). Key constraints the user gave, over several rounds of clarification:

- **Local only, no network API calls, ever** — all computation and data must live on disk.
- **Industrial-level code standards** — proper structure, types, tests — even though it's for local/personal use.
- **Python**, using an existing ephemeris library rather than reimplementing orbital mechanics from JPL kernels.
- Chart output in **South Indian style** (fixed 4x4 grid, signs fixed per cell, ascendant marked) — other styles (North/East Indian) offered as config options, not hard-coded.
- No drag-and-drop UI needed — "moving/shifting of signs" turned out to mean configurable chart style / ayanamsha / house system settings, not an interactive UI.
- MCP server (so Claude/agents can call the chart engine as local tools) should be part of this build, not deferred indefinitely — but built after the core math is solid and tested, since that's the error-prone part.
- Full "kundali essentials" for the first working version: birth chart (D1), houses, nakshatras+pada, Navamsa (D9), Panchanga, Vimshottari Dasha.

This plan covers **Phase 1**: a tested, working core engine + CLI. MCP server and deeper features (more vargas, more dasha systems, shadbala, Western astrology, graph layer) are named as Phase 2/3 but not built now.

## Architecture

Four layers, each independently testable:

1. **Ephemeris layer** — wraps `pyswisseph` (Swiss Ephemeris). Given a UTC datetime + lat/lon, returns raw planetary longitudes. Pure astronomy, no astrology concepts yet. Runs fully offline (Swiss Ephemeris supports a built-in analytical "Moshier" mode requiring zero external data files — this is the default so there is never a download step).
2. **Astrology logic layer** — pure Python, converts raw longitudes into Vedic concepts: rashi (sign), bhava (house, whole-sign system), nakshatra + pada, Navamsa (D9), Panchanga (tithi/vara/nakshatra/yoga/karana), Vimshottari Dasha timeline.
3. **Rendering layer** — turns the computed chart into a South Indian-style chart (fixed-grid text/ASCII layout for Phase 1; North/East Indian and image/SVG rendering are later options via a `style` setting).
4. **Interface layer** — a CLI (Typer) that takes birth date/time/place and prints/exports the chart. MCP server comes after this, as a thin wrapper exposing the same engine functions as tools.

```
Birth data (date, time, lat/lon, tz)
        │
        ▼
 [1] ephemeris.py  ── pyswisseph ──▶ raw planetary longitudes
        │
        ▼
 [2] rashi_bhava.py, nakshatra.py, varga.py, panchanga.py, dasha.py
        │
        ▼
 [3] chart_render.py ──▶ South Indian chart (text) + JSON export
        │
        ▼
 [4] cli.py (Phase 1)  →  mcp_server.py (Phase 2)
```

## Tech stack & why

| Tool | Role | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `pyswisseph` | Ephemeris + sidereal/ayanamsha math | Industry-standard for Vedic astrology, offline-capable (Moshier mode needs no data files), has built-in ayanamsha and house-system support. AGPL-licensed — fine for local/personal use; flagged to the user already. |
| `pydantic` v2 | Typed data models (BirthData, PlanetPosition, KundaliChart, etc.) | Validates inputs/outputs, catches mistakes early, self-documenting |
| `typer` | CLI | Thin, typed CLI on top of the engine functions |
| `pytest` | Test suite | Regression protection for the astrology math, which is easy to get subtly wrong |
| `pyproject.toml` (hatchling backend) | Packaging | Standard, minimal, no extra tooling required |

Timezone/coordinates: Phase 1 takes **latitude, longitude, and UTC offset (or IANA timezone name) as direct input** rather than a place-name geocoder — avoids pulling in a network-based geocoding service. A local place-name → coordinates lookup (offline gazetteer package) is a Phase 2 convenience addition once the core is proven.

Defaults (all overridable via config/CLI flags): **Lahiri (Chitrapaksha) ayanamsha**, **whole-sign house system**, **mean node** for Rahu/Ketu, **South Indian** chart style — these are the conventional defaults used by most Indian Panchangs.

## Project layout

```
notes/
  pyproject.toml
  README.md
  src/
    vedic_astro/
      __init__.py
      models.py          # Pydantic models: BirthData, PlanetPosition, HousePlacement, KundaliChart, PanchangaResult, DashaPeriod
      ephemeris.py        # pyswisseph wrapper: raw planetary longitudes for a UTC datetime + location
      rashi_bhava.py       # sign + whole-sign house assignment, ascendant/lagna calculation
      nakshatra.py         # nakshatra + pada lookup from longitude
      varga.py             # divisional charts, starting with Navamsa (D9)
      panchanga.py         # tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga, karana for a date/place
      dasha.py             # Vimshottari Dasha (starting balance + full sequence, current active period)
      chart_render.py      # South Indian (default) / North / East Indian text chart rendering
      cli.py               # Typer CLI entry point
  tests/
    test_ephemeris.py
    test_rashi_bhava.py
    test_nakshatra.py
    test_varga.py
    test_panchanga.py
    test_dasha.py
    test_chart_render.py
```

Package name: `vedic_astro` (easy to rename later if the user wants a different project name).

## Build order (each step runs and is checkable before moving on)

1. **`models.py` + `ephemeris.py`** — define the core data shapes, then wrap `pyswisseph` to return raw planetary longitudes (Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, Ketu) for a given UTC datetime + lat/lon, in sidereal mode with Lahiri ayanamsha.
   - *Verify:* run against a known birth datetime, cross-check planetary degrees against a trusted reference chart (e.g. the user's own known chart from an existing trusted app).
2. **`rashi_bhava.py`** — compute ascendant (lagna), assign each planet a rashi (sign) and bhava (house, whole-sign).
   - *Verify:* same reference chart — signs/houses should match.
3. **`nakshatra.py` + `varga.py` (Navamsa/D9)** — nakshatra + pada per planet, D9 chart placement.
4. **`panchanga.py`** — tithi/vara/nakshatra/yoga/karana for the birth date and location.
5. **`dasha.py`** — Vimshottari Dasha: starting nakshatra-lord balance, full 120-year sequence, current active mahadasha/antardasha as of a given date.
6. **`chart_render.py`** — render the full computed chart (steps 2-5) as a South Indian-style text grid, plus JSON export.
7. **`cli.py`** — Typer command taking `--dob`, `--tob`, `--lat`, `--lon`, `--utc-offset` (or `--tz`), printing the rendered chart and optionally writing JSON.
8. **Full pytest suite** covering steps 1-6 against the reference chart(s), run at each step rather than only at the end.

Each numbered step gets its own test file and is confirmed working before the next step starts.

## Deferred to later phases (not built now)

- MCP server exposing engine functions as tools (Phase 2, right after Phase 1 is solid).
- Offline place-name → coordinates lookup (Phase 2).
- Additional divisional charts beyond D9, additional dasha systems, shadbala, aspects (graha drishti), Ashtakoot compatibility (Phase 2/3).
- North/East Indian chart rendering, SVG/image output (Phase 2, config already leaves room for this).
- Western astrology, graph/query layer (Phase 3, only if wanted later).

## Verification plan

- `pytest` run after every module lands (not just at the end).
- Cross-check at least one full chart's output (planet signs, houses, nakshatras, Navamsa, current dasha) against a trusted existing Vedic astrology source using the user's own real birth details, since that's the most meaningful correctness check available without a formal test-oracle dataset.
- CLI smoke test: run `vedic-astro --dob ... --tob ... --lat ... --lon ... --utc-offset ...` and confirm a readable South Indian chart prints correctly.

Timezone/coordinates: Phase 1 takes **latitude, longitude, and UTC offset (or IANA timezone name) as direct input** rather than a place-name geocoder — avoids pulling in a network-based geocoding service. A local place-name → coordinates lookup (offline gazetteer package) is a Phase 2 convenience addition once the core is proven.

Defaults (all overridable via config/CLI flags): **Lahiri (Chitrapaksha) ayanamsha**, **whole-sign house system**, **mean node** for Rahu/Ketu, **South Indian** chart style — these are the conventional defaults used by most Indian Panchangs.

## Project layout

```
notes/
  pyproject.toml
  README.md
  src/
    vedic_astro/
      __init__.py
      models.py          # Pydantic models: BirthData, PlanetPosition, HousePlacement, KundaliChart, PanchangaResult, DashaPeriod
      ephemeris.py        # pyswisseph wrapper: raw planetary longitudes for a UTC datetime + location
      rashi_bhava.py       # sign + whole-sign house assignment, ascendant/lagna calculation
      nakshatra.py         # nakshatra + pada lookup from longitude
      varga.py             # divisional charts, starting with Navamsa (D9)
      panchanga.py         # tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga, karana for a date/place
      dasha.py             # Vimshottari Dasha (starting balance + full sequence, current active period)
      chart_render.py      # South Indian (default) / North / East Indian chart layout logic (HTML-ready structure)
      web/
        app.py             # FastAPI app: GET shows the empty form, POST computes + re-renders with the chart
        templates/
          index.html        # single page: form + chart grid, rendered via Jinja2
        static/
          style.css          # South Indian grid styling
  tests/
    test_ephemeris.py
    test_rashi_bhava.py
    test_nakshatra.py
    test_varga.py
    test_panchanga.py
    test_dasha.py
    test_chart_render.py
    test_web_app.py       # FastAPI TestClient: form submission returns a correctly rendered chart
```

Package name: `vedic_astro` (easy to rename later if the user wants a different project name).

## Build order (each step runs and is checkable before moving on)

1. **`models.py` + `ephemeris.py`** — define the core data shapes, then wrap `pyswisseph` to return raw planetary longitudes (Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, Ketu) for a given UTC datetime + lat/lon, in sidereal mode with Lahiri ayanamsha.
   - *Verify:* run against a known birth datetime, cross-check planetary degrees against a trusted reference chart (e.g. the user's own known chart from an existing trusted app).
2. **`rashi_bhava.py`** — compute ascendant (lagna), assign each planet a rashi (sign) and bhava (house, whole-sign).
   - *Verify:* same reference chart — signs/houses should match.
3. **`nakshatra.py` + `varga.py` (Navamsa/D9)** — nakshatra + pada per planet, D9 chart placement.
4. **`panchanga.py`** — tithi/vara/nakshatra/yoga/karana for the birth date and location.
5. **`dasha.py`** — Vimshottari Dasha: starting nakshatra-lord balance, full 120-year sequence, current active mahadasha/antardasha as of a given date.
6. **`chart_render.py`** — structure the full computed chart (steps 2-5) into the fixed South Indian grid layout (which sign goes in which of the 12 cells, ascendant marked, planets placed).
7. **`web/app.py` + `templates/index.html`** — FastAPI app with one route: `GET /` shows the birth-data form (date, time, latitude, longitude, UTC offset), `POST /` computes the chart and re-renders the same page with the South Indian grid (HTML/CSS) plus nakshatra/panchanga/dasha info below it. Run locally with `uvicorn` — opens in your browser at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`.
8. **Full pytest suite** covering steps 1-7 against the reference chart(s), run at each step rather than only at the end.

Each numbered step gets its own test file and is confirmed working before the next step starts.

## Deferred to later phases (not built now)

- MCP server exposing engine functions as tools (Phase 2, right after Phase 1 is solid).
- Offline place-name → coordinates lookup (Phase 2).
- Additional divisional charts beyond D9, additional dasha systems, shadbala, aspects (graha drishti), Ashtakoot compatibility (Phase 2/3).
- North/East Indian chart rendering, SVG/image output (Phase 2, config already leaves room for this).
- Western astrology, graph/query layer (Phase 3, only if wanted later).

## Verification plan

- `pytest` run after every module lands (not just at the end).
- Cross-check at least one full chart's output (planet signs, houses, nakshatras, Navamsa, current dasha) against a trusted existing Vedic astrology source using the user's own real birth details, since that's the most meaningful correctness check available without a formal test-oracle dataset.
- Web smoke test: run the FastAPI app locally (`uvicorn vedic_astro.web.app:app --reload`), open `http://127.0.0.1:8000` in a browser, submit real birth details on the one-screen form, and confirm the South Indian chart renders correctly with all sections (planets, houses, nakshatras, Navamsa, panchanga, dasha).

# vedic-astro

and location on a single web page and get a South Indian-style kundali:
planets, houses, nakshatras, Navamsa (D9), Panchanga, and Vimshottari Dasha.

pip install -e ".[dev]"

```bash
uvicorn vedic_astro.web.app:app --reload
```

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in a browser.

## Run tests

```bash
pytest
```

## Defaults

- Ayanamsha: Lahiri (Chitrapaksha)
- House system: Whole sign
- Rahu/Ketu: Mean node
- Chart style: South Indian

    chart_style: ChartStyle = ChartStyle.SOUTH_INDIAN

    def local_datetime(self) -> datetime:
        return datetime.combine(self.birth_date, self.birth_time)

    @property
    def utc_datetime(self) -> datetime:
        return self.local_datetime - timedelta(hours=self.utc_offset_hours)


class NakshatraPlacement(BaseModel):
    name: str
    index: int = Field(ge=1, le=27)
    pada: int = Field(ge=1, le=4)
    lord: Planet

    longitude: float = Field(ge=0, lt=360)
    sign: Sign

    planet: Planet
    longitude: float = Field(ge=0, lt=360)

    end: datetime

    start: datetime
    end: datetime
    sub_periods: list[DashaSubPeriod]

    def current_mahadasha(self, at: datetime) -> DashaPeriod | None:
        for period in self.periods:

        return None

    def current_antardasha(self, at: datetime) -> DashaSubPeriod | None:

        if maha is None:

        for sub in maha.sub_periods:
            if sub.start <= at < sub.end:

        return None


class KundaliChart(BaseModel):
    birth_data: BirthData
    ascendant: Ascendant
    planets: list[PlanetPosition]
    panchanga: PanchangaResult
    dasha: VimshottariDasha

"""Thin wrapper around pyswisseph: raw sidereal planetary longitudes only.

No astrology concepts (signs, houses, nakshatras) live here - just "where is
this body, in degrees, right now". Runs fully offline: FLG_MOSEPH selects
Swiss Ephemeris' built-in analytical model, which needs no external data
files (no download, no network call, ever).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime

import swisseph as swe

from vedic_astro.models import NodeType, Planet

_AYANAMSHA_MODES: dict[str, int] = {
    "lahiri": swe.SIDM_LAHIRI,
    "raman": swe.SIDM_RAMAN,
    "krishnamurti": swe.SIDM_KRISHNAMURTI,
}

_SWE_PLANET_IDS: dict[Planet, int] = {
    Planet.SUN: swe.SUN,
    Planet.MOON: swe.MOON,
    Planet.MARS: swe.MARS,
    Planet.MERCURY: swe.MERCURY,
    Planet.JUPITER: swe.JUPITER,
    Planet.VENUS: swe.VENUS,
    Planet.SATURN: swe.SATURN,
}

_CALC_FLAGS = swe.FLG_SIDEREAL | swe.FLG_SPEED | swe.FLG_MOSEPH


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RawPosition:
    """A body's sidereal ecliptic longitude and daily motion, nothing else."""

    longitude: float  # degrees, 0-360
    speed_longitude: float  # degrees/day; negative means retrograde

    @property
    def retrograde(self) -> bool:
        return self.speed_longitude < 0


def julian_day_ut(utc_dt: datetime) -> float:
    hour = utc_dt.hour + utc_dt.minute / 60 + utc_dt.second / 3600
    return swe.julday(utc_dt.year, utc_dt.month, utc_dt.day, hour)


def configure_ayanamsha(ayanamsha: str) -> None:
    mode = _AYANAMSHA_MODES.get(ayanamsha.lower())
    if mode is None:
        known = ", ".join(sorted(_AYANAMSHA_MODES))
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported ayanamsha {ayanamsha!r}; known: {known}")
    swe.set_sid_mode(mode)


def planet_positions(
    utc_dt: datetime, ayanamsha: str, node_type: NodeType
) -> dict[Planet, RawPosition]:
    """Sidereal longitude + speed for all 9 grahas at the given UTC moment."""
    configure_ayanamsha(ayanamsha)
    jd = julian_day_ut(utc_dt)

    positions: dict[Planet, RawPosition] = {}
    for planet, swe_id in _SWE_PLANET_IDS.items():
        values, _flags = swe.calc_ut(jd, swe_id, _CALC_FLAGS)
        lon, _lat, _dist, lon_speed, _lat_speed, _dist_speed = values
        positions[planet] = RawPosition(longitude=lon % 360, speed_longitude=lon_speed)

    node_id = swe.MEAN_NODE if node_type == NodeType.MEAN else swe.TRUE_NODE
    node_values, _flags = swe.calc_ut(jd, node_id, _CALC_FLAGS)
    rahu_lon, _lat, _dist, rahu_speed, _lat_speed, _dist_speed = node_values
    positions[Planet.RAHU] = RawPosition(longitude=rahu_lon % 360, speed_longitude=rahu_speed)
    # Ketu is always exactly opposite Rahu - not an independent body in Swiss Ephemeris.
    positions[Planet.KETU] = RawPosition(
        longitude=(rahu_lon + 180) % 360, speed_longitude=rahu_speed
    )

    return positions


def ascendant_longitude(
    utc_dt: datetime, latitude: float, longitude: float, ayanamsha: str
) -> float:
    """Sidereal longitude of the ascendant (lagna), 0-360 degrees."""
    configure_ayanamsha(ayanamsha)
    jd = julian_day_ut(utc_dt)
    _cusps, ascmc = swe.houses_ex(jd, latitude, longitude, b"W", swe.FLG_SIDEREAL)
    return ascmc[0] % 360

from datetime import datetime

import pytest

from vedic_astro.ephemeris import ascendant_longitude, julian_day_ut, planet_positions
from vedic_astro.models import NodeType, Planet


def test_julian_day_matches_known_epoch() -> None:
    # J2000.0 epoch: 2000-01-01 12:00 UT -> JD 2451545.0 exactly.
    assert julian_day_ut(datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0)) == pytest.approx(2451545.0)


def test_planet_positions_returns_all_nine_grahas() -> None:
    positions = planet_positions(datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0), "lahiri", NodeType.MEAN)
    assert set(positions) == {
        Planet.SUN,
        Planet.MOON,
        Planet.MARS,
        Planet.MERCURY,
        Planet.JUPITER,
        Planet.VENUS,
        Planet.SATURN,
        Planet.RAHU,
        Planet.KETU,
    }
    for pos in positions.values():
        assert 0 <= pos.longitude < 360


def test_sun_sidereal_longitude_matches_known_lahiri_value() -> None:
    # Published Lahiri-ayanamsha sidereal Sun longitude for 2000-01-01 12:00 UT
    # is ~256.5 degrees (tropical ~280.3 minus ayanamsha ~23.85).
    positions = planet_positions(datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0), "lahiri", NodeType.MEAN)
    assert positions[Planet.SUN].longitude == pytest.approx(256.5, abs=0.1)


def test_rahu_and_ketu_are_always_opposite() -> None:
    positions = planet_positions(datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0), "lahiri", NodeType.MEAN)
    rahu = positions[Planet.RAHU].longitude
    ketu = positions[Planet.KETU].longitude
    assert (rahu + 180) % 360 == pytest.approx(ketu, abs=1e-9)


def test_ascendant_longitude_in_valid_range() -> None:
    asc = ascendant_longitude(datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0), 28.6139, 77.2090, "lahiri")
    assert 0 <= asc < 360


def test_unsupported_ayanamsha_raises() -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Unsupported ayanamsha"):
        planet_positions(datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0), "not-a-real-one", NodeType.MEAN)

"""Sign (rashi) and whole-sign house (bhava) assignment from ecliptic longitude."""

from __future__ import annotations

from vedic_astro.models import SIGNS_IN_ORDER, Ascendant, Sign


def sign_for_longitude(longitude: float) -> Sign:
    index = int(longitude // 30) % 12
    return SIGNS_IN_ORDER[index]


def degree_in_sign(longitude: float) -> float:
    return longitude % 30


def whole_sign_house(planet_sign: Sign, ascendant_sign: Sign) -> int:
    """House number (1-12) under the whole-sign system.

    The ascendant's sign is house 1 in its entirety; every other sign is
    simply counted forward from there - there is no sub-division by degree.
    """
    asc_index = SIGNS_IN_ORDER.index(ascendant_sign)
    planet_index = SIGNS_IN_ORDER.index(planet_sign)
    return ((planet_index - asc_index) % 12) + 1


def build_ascendant(longitude: float) -> Ascendant:
    return Ascendant(
        longitude=longitude,
        sign=sign_for_longitude(longitude),
        degree_in_sign=degree_in_sign(longitude),
    )

@pytest.mark.parametrize(

        (29.99, Sign.ARIES),
        (30.0, Sign.TAURUS),

        (359.99, Sign.PISCES),

from vedic_astro.models import NakshatraPlacement, Planet

NAKSHATRA_SPAN = 360 / 27  # 13d20', one nakshatra
PADA_SPAN = NAKSHATRA_SPAN / 4  # 3d20', one pada

    "Ashwini", "Bharani", "Krittika", "Rohini", "Mrigashira", "Ardra",

    "Purva Bhadrapada", "Uttara Bhadrapada", "Revati",
]

_DASHA_LORD_CYCLE: list[Planet] = [
    Planet.KETU, Planet.VENUS, Planet.SUN, Planet.MOON, Planet.MARS,
    Planet.RAHU, Planet.JUPITER, Planet.SATURN, Planet.MERCURY,
]

        index=index + 1,
        pada=pada,
        lord=NAKSHATRA_LORDS[index],

from __future__ import annotations

from vedic_astro.models import SIGNS_IN_ORDER, Sign

NAVAMSA_DIVISIONS = 108  # 12 signs x 9 navamsas per sign
NAVAMSA_SPAN = 360 / NAVAMSA_DIVISIONS  # 3d20', same width as a nakshatra pada
_EPSILON = 1e-9


def navamsa_sign(longitude: float) -> Sign:
    """D9 sign for a given sidereal longitude.

    Equivalent to the classical movable/fixed/dual starting-sign rule, but
    expressed as one continuous 108-division cycle around the whole zodiac -
    the two are mathematically the same, this form is just easier to get
    right in code.
    """
    longitude = longitude % 360
    division_index = min(int((longitude + _EPSILON) // NAVAMSA_SPAN), NAVAMSA_DIVISIONS - 1)
    return SIGNS_IN_ORDER[division_index % 12]

from vedic_astro.nakshatra import NAKSHATRA_SPAN, nakshatra_for_longitude

    n = nakshatra_for_longitude(0.0)
    assert n.name == "Ashwini"
    assert n.index == 1
    assert n.pada == 1
    assert n.lord == Planet.KETU


def test_revati_near_360_degrees() -> None:
    n = nakshatra_for_longitude(359.9)
    assert n.name == "Revati"
    assert n.index == 27
    assert n.pada == 4
    assert n.lord == Planet.MERCURY


def test_wraps_at_360() -> None:

    n = nakshatra_for_longitude(longitude)
    assert n.index == boundary_index + 1
    assert n.pada == 1


def test_pada_progression_within_a_nakshatra() -> None:
    # Bharani spans 13.3333-26.6667 degrees; check all four pada boundaries.
    start = NAKSHATRA_SPAN  # start of Bharani
    pada_span = NAKSHATRA_SPAN / 4
    for pada_number in range(1, 5):

"""Panchanga: the 5 daily almanac elements, computed at the birth moment.

Tithi/yoga/karana/nakshatra are derived from the birth-moment Sun and Moon
longitudes (the standard approach for a natal chart's panchanga, as opposed
to a general daily almanac which is anchored to sunrise). Vara (weekday) is
taken from the civil calendar date - a known simplification versus the
traditional sunrise-to-sunrise day boundary, acceptable for Phase 1.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import date

from vedic_astro.models import PanchangaElement, PanchangaResult
from vedic_astro.nakshatra import nakshatra_for_longitude

TITHI_SPAN = 12.0
KARANA_SPAN = 6.0
YOGA_SPAN = 360 / 27
_EPSILON = 1e-9

TITHI_NAMES: list[str] = [
    "Pratipada", "Dwitiya", "Tritiya", "Chaturthi", "Panchami", "Shashthi",
    "Saptami", "Ashtami", "Navami", "Dashami", "Ekadashi", "Dwadashi",
    "Trayodashi", "Chaturdashi",
]

YOGA_NAMES: list[str] = [
    "Vishkambha", "Priti", "Ayushman", "Saubhagya", "Shobhana", "Atiganda",
    "Sukarma", "Dhriti", "Shula", "Ganda", "Vriddhi", "Dhruva", "Vyaghata",
    "Harshana", "Vajra", "Siddhi", "Vyatipata", "Variyana", "Parigha", "Shiva",
    "Siddha", "Sadhya", "Shubha", "Shukla", "Brahma", "Indra", "Vaidhriti",
]

MOVABLE_KARANA_NAMES: list[str] = [
    "Bava", "Balava", "Kaulava", "Taitila", "Gara", "Vanija", "Vishti",
]

# Indexed by date.weekday() (Monday=0 ... Sunday=6).
VARA_NAMES: list[str] = [
    "Somavara", "Mangalavara", "Budhavara", "Guruvara", "Shukravara", "Shanivara", "Ravivara",
]


def _tithi(sun_longitude: float, moon_longitude: float) -> tuple[PanchangaElement, str]:
    diff = (moon_longitude - sun_longitude) % 360
    index = min(int((diff + _EPSILON) // TITHI_SPAN), 29)
    paksha = "Shukla" if index < 15 else "Krishna"
    within_paksha = (index % 15) + 1
    name = TITHI_NAMES[within_paksha - 1] if within_paksha <= 14 else (
        "Purnima" if paksha == "Shukla" else "Amavasya"
    )
    return PanchangaElement(name=name, index=index + 1), paksha


def _karana(sun_longitude: float, moon_longitude: float) -> PanchangaElement:
    diff = (moon_longitude - sun_longitude) % 360
    index = min(int((diff + _EPSILON) // KARANA_SPAN), 59)
    if index == 0:
        name = "Kimstughna"
    elif index <= 56:
        name = MOVABLE_KARANA_NAMES[(index - 1) % 7]
    elif index == 57:
        name = "Shakuni"
    elif index == 58:
        name = "Chatushpada"
    else:
        name = "Naga"
    return PanchangaElement(name=name, index=index + 1)


def _yoga(sun_longitude: float, moon_longitude: float) -> PanchangaElement:
    diff = (sun_longitude + moon_longitude) % 360
    index = min(int((diff + _EPSILON) // YOGA_SPAN), 26)
    return PanchangaElement(name=YOGA_NAMES[index], index=index + 1)


def _vara(local_date: date) -> str:
    return VARA_NAMES[local_date.weekday()]


def compute_panchanga(
    sun_longitude: float, moon_longitude: float, local_date: date
) -> PanchangaResult:
    tithi, paksha = _tithi(sun_longitude, moon_longitude)
    moon_nakshatra = nakshatra_for_longitude(moon_longitude)
    return PanchangaResult(
        tithi=tithi,
        paksha=paksha,
        vara=_vara(local_date),
        nakshatra=PanchangaElement(name=moon_nakshatra.name, index=moon_nakshatra.index),
        yoga=_yoga(sun_longitude, moon_longitude),
        karana=_karana(sun_longitude, moon_longitude),
    )

from datetime import date

import pytest

from vedic_astro.panchanga import compute_panchanga


def test_new_moon_is_amavasya_tithi_thirty() -> None:
    # Sun and Moon at the same longitude -> diff 0 -> first tithi of Krishna... actually
    # diff=0 is the *start* of Shukla Pratipada (new moon moment itself, tithi 1).
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=100.0, moon_longitude=100.0, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.tithi.name == "Pratipada"
    assert result.paksha == "Shukla"
    assert result.tithi.index == 1


def test_full_moon_is_purnima() -> None:
    # Moon exactly 180 degrees from Sun -> full moon -> tithi 15, Purnima.
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=100.0, moon_longitude=280.0, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.tithi.name == "Purnima"
    assert result.paksha == "Shukla"
    assert result.tithi.index == 15


def test_just_before_new_moon_is_amavasya() -> None:
    # Moon just short of a full 360-degree catch-up -> last tithi, Krishna Amavasya.
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=100.0, moon_longitude=99.5, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.tithi.name == "Amavasya"
    assert result.paksha == "Krishna"
    assert result.tithi.index == 30


def test_karana_kimstughna_at_zero_diff() -> None:
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=50.0, moon_longitude=50.0, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.karana.name == "Kimstughna"


def test_karana_movable_cycle() -> None:
    # 6 degrees into the diff -> second karana slot (index 1, 0-indexed) -> first movable, Bava.
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=0.0, moon_longitude=6.0, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.karana.name == "Bava"


def test_yoga_first_slot_is_vishkambha() -> None:
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=0.0, moon_longitude=0.0, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.yoga.name == "Vishkambha"
    assert result.yoga.index == 1


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("year", "month", "day", "expected_vara"),
    [
        (2024, 1, 1, "Somavara"),  # Monday
        (2024, 1, 7, "Ravivara"),  # Sunday
    ],
)
def test_vara_matches_calendar_weekday(year: int, month: int, day: int, expected_vara: str) -> None:
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=0.0, moon_longitude=0.0, local_date=date(year, month, day))
    assert result.vara == expected_vara


def test_nakshatra_reflects_moon_position() -> None:
    result = compute_panchanga(sun_longitude=0.0, moon_longitude=0.0, local_date=date(2024, 1, 1))
    assert result.nakshatra.name == "Ashwini"

"""Nakshatra (lunar mansion) and pada lookup from sidereal ecliptic longitude."""

from __future__ import annotations

from vedic_astro.models import NakshatraPlacement, Planet

NAKSHATRA_SPAN = 360 / 27  # 13d20', one nakshatra
PADA_SPAN = NAKSHATRA_SPAN / 4  # 3d20', one pada
_EPSILON = 1e-9  # guards float boundary rounding right at a nakshatra/pada edge

NAKSHATRA_NAMES: list[str] = [
    "Ashwini", "Bharani", "Krittika", "Rohini", "Mrigashira", "Ardra",
    "Punarvasu", "Pushya", "Ashlesha", "Magha", "Purva Phalguni", "Uttara Phalguni",
    "Hasta", "Chitra", "Swati", "Vishakha", "Anuradha", "Jyeshtha",
    "Mula", "Purva Ashadha", "Uttara Ashadha", "Shravana", "Dhanishta", "Shatabhisha",
    "Purva Bhadrapada", "Uttara Bhadrapada", "Revati",
]

# Vimshottari dasha lord cycle, repeated 3x to cover all 27 nakshatras.
_DASHA_LORD_CYCLE: list[Planet] = [
    Planet.KETU, Planet.VENUS, Planet.SUN, Planet.MOON, Planet.MARS,
    Planet.RAHU, Planet.JUPITER, Planet.SATURN, Planet.MERCURY,
]
NAKSHATRA_LORDS: list[Planet] = _DASHA_LORD_CYCLE * 3


def nakshatra_for_longitude(longitude: float) -> NakshatraPlacement:
    longitude = longitude % 360
    index = min(int((longitude + _EPSILON) // NAKSHATRA_SPAN), 26)
    within_nakshatra = longitude - index * NAKSHATRA_SPAN
    pada = min(int((within_nakshatra + _EPSILON) // PADA_SPAN) + 1, 4)
    return NakshatraPlacement(
        name=NAKSHATRA_NAMES[index],
        index=index + 1,
        pada=pada,
        lord=NAKSHATRA_LORDS[index],
    )

"""Vimshottari Dasha: the 120-year planetary period timeline.

The mahadasha (major period) in effect at birth is determined by the Moon's
nakshatra lord and how far the Moon already was through that nakshatra; the
remaining 8 mahadashas follow in the fixed cycle, each subdivided into 9
antardashas (sub-periods) using the standard proportional formula.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import datetime, timedelta

from vedic_astro.models import DashaPeriod, DashaSubPeriod, Planet, VimshottariDasha
from vedic_astro.nakshatra import DASHA_LORD_CYCLE, NAKSHATRA_SPAN, nakshatra_for_longitude

DAYS_PER_YEAR = 365.2425  # average Gregorian year

DASHA_YEARS: dict[Planet, float] = {
    Planet.KETU: 7, Planet.VENUS: 20, Planet.SUN: 6, Planet.MOON: 10,
    Planet.MARS: 7, Planet.RAHU: 18, Planet.JUPITER: 16, Planet.SATURN: 19,
    Planet.MERCURY: 17,
}

TOTAL_CYCLE_YEARS = sum(DASHA_YEARS.values())  # 120


def _years_to_timedelta(years: float) -> timedelta:
    return timedelta(days=years * DAYS_PER_YEAR)


def _antardashas(
    mahadasha_lord: Planet, start: datetime, mahadasha_years: float
) -> list[DashaSubPeriod]:
    start_index = DASHA_LORD_CYCLE.index(mahadasha_lord)
    sub_periods: list[DashaSubPeriod] = []
    cursor = start
    for offset in range(9):
        sub_lord = DASHA_LORD_CYCLE[(start_index + offset) % 9]
        sub_years = mahadasha_years * DASHA_YEARS[sub_lord] / TOTAL_CYCLE_YEARS
        sub_end = cursor + _years_to_timedelta(sub_years)
        sub_periods.append(DashaSubPeriod(planet=sub_lord, start=cursor, end=sub_end))
        cursor = sub_end
    return sub_periods


def compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude: float, birth_datetime: datetime) -> VimshottariDasha:
    moon_longitude = moon_longitude % 360
    nakshatra = nakshatra_for_longitude(moon_longitude)
    elapsed_within_nakshatra = moon_longitude - (nakshatra.index - 1) * NAKSHATRA_SPAN
    elapsed_fraction = max(0.0, min(1.0, elapsed_within_nakshatra / NAKSHATRA_SPAN))

    first_lord = nakshatra.lord
    first_lord_years = DASHA_YEARS[first_lord]
    elapsed_years = elapsed_fraction * first_lord_years
    first_start = birth_datetime - _years_to_timedelta(elapsed_years)

    start_index = DASHA_LORD_CYCLE.index(first_lord)
    periods: list[DashaPeriod] = []
    cursor = first_start
    for offset in range(9):
        lord = DASHA_LORD_CYCLE[(start_index + offset) % 9]
        lord_years = DASHA_YEARS[lord]
        period_end = cursor + _years_to_timedelta(lord_years)
        periods.append(
            DashaPeriod(
                planet=lord,
                start=cursor,
                end=period_end,
                sub_periods=_antardashas(lord, cursor, lord_years),
            )
        )
        cursor = period_end

    return VimshottariDasha(periods=periods)

from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import pytest

from vedic_astro.dasha import DASHA_YEARS, DAYS_PER_YEAR, TOTAL_CYCLE_YEARS, compute_vimshottari_dasha
from vedic_astro.models import Planet
from vedic_astro.nakshatra import DASHA_LORD_CYCLE, NAKSHATRA_SPAN


def test_moon_at_nakshatra_start_gives_full_first_mahadasha() -> None:
    birth = datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0)
    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude=0.0, birth_datetime=birth)  # start of Ashwini
    first = dasha.periods[0]
    assert first.planet == Planet.KETU  # Ashwini's lord
    assert first.start == pytest.approx(birth.timestamp(), abs=1) if False else True
    # start should equal birth (no balance already elapsed before birth)
    assert abs((first.start - birth).total_seconds()) < 1
    expected_years = DASHA_YEARS[Planet.KETU]
    expected_end = birth + timedelta(days=expected_years * DAYS_PER_YEAR)
    assert abs((first.end - expected_end).total_seconds()) < 1


def test_moon_near_nakshatra_end_gives_almost_no_balance() -> None:
    birth = datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0)
    almost_end = NAKSHATRA_SPAN * 0.999  # just before Ashwini ends
    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude=almost_end, birth_datetime=birth)
    first = dasha.periods[0]
    # Almost the entire Ketu mahadasha has already elapsed before birth.
    remaining_days = (first.end - birth).days
    assert 0 <= remaining_days < 10


def test_mahadasha_order_follows_fixed_cycle_from_nakshatra_lord() -> None:
    birth = datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0)
    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude=0.0, birth_datetime=birth)
    lords = [p.planet for p in dasha.periods]
    start_index = DASHA_LORD_CYCLE.index(Planet.KETU)
    expected = [DASHA_LORD_CYCLE[(start_index + i) % 9] for i in range(9)]
    assert lords == expected


def test_periods_are_contiguous_and_cover_full_120_years() -> None:
    birth = datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0)
    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude=45.0, birth_datetime=birth)
    for earlier, later in zip(dasha.periods, dasha.periods[1:]):
        assert earlier.end == later.start
    total_days = (dasha.periods[-1].end - dasha.periods[0].start).days
    expected_days = TOTAL_CYCLE_YEARS * DAYS_PER_YEAR
    assert abs(total_days - expected_days) < 2


def test_antardashas_sum_to_mahadasha_span() -> None:
    birth = datetime(2000, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0)
    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude=0.0, birth_datetime=birth)
    for period in dasha.periods:
        assert period.sub_periods[0].start == period.start
        assert period.sub_periods[-1].end == period.end
        assert len(period.sub_periods) == 9
        for earlier, later in zip(period.sub_periods, period.sub_periods[1:]):

    first_mahadasha = dasha.periods[0]
    assert first_mahadasha.sub_periods[0].planet == first_mahadasha.planet

    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(moon_longitude=0.0, birth_datetime=birth)

"""Composition root: wires ephemeris + astrology-logic modules into one KundaliChart."""

from __future__ import annotations

from vedic_astro.dasha import compute_vimshottari_dasha
from vedic_astro.ephemeris import ascendant_longitude, planet_positions
from vedic_astro.models import BirthData, KundaliChart, Planet, PlanetPosition
from vedic_astro.nakshatra import nakshatra_for_longitude
from vedic_astro.panchanga import compute_panchanga
from vedic_astro.rashi_bhava import build_ascendant, degree_in_sign, sign_for_longitude, whole_sign_house
from vedic_astro.varga import navamsa_sign


def build_kundali_chart(birth_data: BirthData) -> KundaliChart:
    utc_dt = birth_data.utc_datetime
    raw_positions = planet_positions(utc_dt, birth_data.ayanamsha, birth_data.node_type)
    asc_longitude = ascendant_longitude(
        utc_dt, birth_data.latitude, birth_data.longitude, birth_data.ayanamsha
    )
    ascendant = build_ascendant(asc_longitude)

    planets: list[PlanetPosition] = []
    # raw_positions preserves the conventional Navagraha order (Sun..Saturn, Rahu, Ketu).
    for planet, raw in raw_positions.items():
        sign = sign_for_longitude(raw.longitude)
        planets.append(
            PlanetPosition(
                planet=planet,
                longitude=raw.longitude,
                sign=sign,
                degree_in_sign=degree_in_sign(raw.longitude),
                house=whole_sign_house(sign, ascendant.sign),
                nakshatra=nakshatra_for_longitude(raw.longitude),
                retrograde=raw.retrograde,
                navamsa_sign=navamsa_sign(raw.longitude),
            )
        )

    moon_longitude = raw_positions[Planet.MOON].longitude
    panchanga = compute_panchanga(
        sun_longitude=raw_positions[Planet.SUN].longitude,
        moon_longitude=moon_longitude,
        local_date=birth_data.birth_date,
    )
    dasha = compute_vimshottari_dasha(
        moon_longitude=moon_longitude, birth_datetime=birth_data.local_datetime
    )

    return KundaliChart(
        birth_data=birth_data,
        ascendant=ascendant,
        planets=planets,
        panchanga=panchanga,
        dasha=dasha,
    )

"""Single-screen local web UI: one form, one rendered South Indian chart.

Runs entirely on localhost via uvicorn - the browser only ever talks to this
process on your own machine, never the internet.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import date, datetime, time, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi import FastAPI, Form, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
from pydantic import ValidationError

from vedic_astro.chart import build_kundali_chart
from vedic_astro.chart_render import south_indian_layout
from vedic_astro.models import BirthData, KundaliChart, NodeType

_BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

app = FastAPI(title="vedic-astro")
app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory=_BASE_DIR / "static"), name="static")
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory=_BASE_DIR / "templates")

_AYANAMSHA_CHOICES = ["lahiri", "raman", "krishnamurti"]


def _current_local_datetime(utc_offset_hours: float) -> datetime:
    """'Now', expressed as a naive datetime in the birth place's local time -
    consistent with the naive local datetimes used throughout the dasha math."""
    now_utc = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(tzinfo=None)
    return now_utc + timedelta(hours=utc_offset_hours)


def _empty_form_context() -> dict[str, object]:
    return {
        "ayanamsha_choices": _AYANAMSHA_CHOICES,
        "form_values": {
            "birth_date": "",
            "birth_time": "",
            "latitude": "",
            "longitude": "",
            "utc_offset_hours": "",
            "ayanamsha": "lahiri",
            "node_type": "mean",
        },
        "chart": None,
        "grid": None,
        "current_mahadasha": None,
        "current_antardasha": None,
        "error": None,
    }


@app.get("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
def show_form(request: Request) -> HTMLResponse:
    context = _empty_form_context()
    return templates.TemplateResponse(request, "index.html", context)


@app.post("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
def compute_chart(
    request: Request,
    birth_date: str = Form(...),
    birth_time: str = Form(...),
    latitude: float = Form(...),
    longitude: float = Form(...),
    utc_offset_hours: float = Form(...),
    ayanamsha: str = Form("lahiri"),
    node_type: str = Form("mean"),
) -> HTMLResponse:
    context = _empty_form_context()
    context["form_values"] = {
        "birth_date": birth_date,
        "birth_time": birth_time,
        "latitude": latitude,
        "longitude": longitude,
        "utc_offset_hours": utc_offset_hours,
        "ayanamsha": ayanamsha,
        "node_type": node_type,
    }

    try:
        parsed_date = date.fromisoformat(birth_date)
        parsed_time = time.fromisoformat(birth_time)
        birth_data = BirthData(
            birth_date=parsed_date,
            birth_time=parsed_time,
            latitude=latitude,
            longitude=longitude,
            utc_offset_hours=utc_offset_hours,
            ayanamsha=ayanamsha,
            node_type=NodeType(node_type),
        )
        chart: KundaliChart = build_kundali_chart(birth_data)
    except (ValueError, ValidationError) as exc:
        context["error"] = str(exc)
        return templates.TemplateResponse(request, "index.html", context, status_code=400)

    now_local = _current_local_datetime(utc_offset_hours)
    context["chart"] = chart
    context["grid"] = south_indian_layout(chart)
    context["current_mahadasha"] = chart.dasha.current_mahadasha(now_local)
    context["current_antardasha"] = chart.dasha.current_antardasha(now_local)
    return templates.TemplateResponse(request, "index.html", context)
